findings.title: `organization_context.member` can be None, causing a 500 on every audit-log request
findings.body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated unconditionally for every GET, before it is known whether the optimized path is even requested. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `RpcOrganizationMember | None` and is None whenever the caller is not an organization member of record — e.g. requests authenticated with an organization auth token / API token that carries `org:write`/`org:admin`, which `OrganizationAuditPermission` accepts. For those callers `request.user.is_superuser` is False (AnonymousUser), so the right-hand side is evaluated and raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'`, turning a previously working endpoint into a hard 500. At minimum the check must be guarded (`organization_context.member and ...`) and only evaluated when `use_optimized` is true.

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator is an integer paginator but is used with a datetime sort key
findings.body: The endpoint sorts by `-datetime` (a `DateTimeField`). `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(getattr(item, self.key)))` and `value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` unchanged — i.e. the integer semantics of `Paginator`, not the millisecond-timestamp conversion that `DateTimePaginator` implements. Consequently, when `optimized_pagination=true` is honored, `build_cursor` calls `get_item_key` on a `datetime` and raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`, and any follow-up cursor value is injected raw into the `WHERE datetime >= %s` clause built by `build_queryset`, comparing an integer against a timestamp column. The optimized path therefore cannot work for this endpoint at all; it only produces 500s (and would silently mis-page if it did not crash).

findings.title: Negative offsets are passed straight into a Django queryset slice and raise ValueError
findings.body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly rejects this with `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` for any slice whose start or stop is negative, so the request ends in an unhandled exception / HTTP 500. The inline comment “The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically” is factually wrong, and the comment “enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds … safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level” documents behaviour that does not exist. Since `Cursor.from_string` accepts any integer offset from the `cursor` query parameter, this is a user-triggerable error path. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError` instead.

findings.title: Silently clamping negative cursor offsets masks invalid cursors and is inconsistent for prev cursors
findings.body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` in `BasePaginator.get_result` silently rewrites an invalid (negative) forward cursor offset to 0, so the caller gets page 1 data while `build_cursor` still derives the next/prev cursors from the original negative `cursor.offset` (e.g. `next_offset = offset + limit`), producing further bogus cursors. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset is still handed to the Django slice, which raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`, so the fix is only half applied. Other paginators in this file (`OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`, `CombinedQuerysetPaginator`) raise `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`; `BasePaginator` should do the same rather than clamp.

findings.title: New OptimizedCursorPaginator has no tests
findings.body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a brand-new public paginator wired into a production endpoint, but no tests were added in this PR (neither for the paginator itself nor for the new `optimized_pagination=true` branch of `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`). As a result the broken datetime key handling and the negative-offset ValueError path described in the other findings would not be caught by CI. Tests should cover: default behaviour parity with `DateTimePaginator` for the audit log ordering, and the behaviour for negative/invalid cursor offsets.

findings.title: Misleading comment added to Cursor.__init__
findings.body: The added comment claims that `self.offset = int(offset)` is a “performance optimization” that “allows negative offsets … enables efficient reverse pagination”. No code changed here; `int(offset)` has always accepted negative values, and negative offsets are not a supported feature — most paginators reject them and Django refuses negative slices. The comment documents a non-existent and unsafe capability and will mislead the next reader into thinking negative offsets are intentional and handled.

findings.title: zunionstore defaults to AGGREGATE SUM, corrupting the end-timestamp scores used for eviction
findings.body: Both merge steps use `redis.call("zunionstore", set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` without an `AGGREGATE` option, so Redis sums the scores of members present in both sorted sets. Scores here are `end_timestamp_precise` values, so a span payload that happens to exist in both the destination set and the merged set (e.g. a duplicate delivery, or a span already zadd'ed under the top-most parent key by `process_spans` and also present under its own span key) ends up with a score of roughly 2×1.7e9. That value is no longer a timestamp, and because the new trimming logic uses `zpopmin` (lowest score evicted first), duplicated spans become effectively un-evictable while legitimate newer spans are dropped. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) to keep scores meaningful.

findings.title: Segment span limit hardcoded to 1000 in Lua, conflicting with the now-dead max_segment_spans setting
findings.body: The new eviction uses the literal `1000` in two places (`if span_count > 1000` / `zpopmin set_key, span_count - 1000`), while `SpansBuffer.__init__` still exposes `max_segment_spans: int = 1001`, which this PR leaves completely unused after removing the span-count check in `_load_segment_data`. The effective limit is therefore no longer configurable, differs from the previous 1001 threshold, and the stale constructor parameter will mislead operators who try to tune it. Either pass the configured limit into the script as an ARGV, or remove `max_segment_spans` from the buffer.

findings.title: Redirect-chain depth limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 and the explanatory comment deleted
findings.body: The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`, and the comment explaining the consequence (“theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly”) was removed. With the lower bound, traces whose redirect chains exceed 1000 hops will stop resolving to their real root set and will be emitted as separate, incorrectly split segments. This is a behavioural change unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (eviction on insert), is not mentioned in the description, and now has no comment documenting the limitation.

findings.title: max_segment_spans is now dead code and the over-size-segment metric/log was dropped
findings.body: `_load_segment_data` no longer checks `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans`, so the constructor parameter `max_segment_spans` is unused, and the `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric plus the accompanying `logger.error` are gone. Any dashboards/alerts built on that metric will silently go to zero, and there is no longer any signal when a segment is truncated — trimming now happens silently inside the Lua script. Add an equivalent metric for evicted spans (e.g. the `zpopmin` count) and remove or honor the unused parameter.

findings.title: Module docstring still describes plain Redis sets and no eviction
findings.body: The storage layout changed from Redis sets (`sadd`/`sscan`/`sunionstore`) to sorted sets keyed by `end_timestamp_precise`, and spans are now evicted on insert once a segment exceeds 1000 members, but the module docstring was not updated: step 3 still says “Add the ingested span's payload to the set under `set_key`” and the glossary still says “span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys”. Nothing documents that spans can now be silently dropped from a segment, which is the most important semantic change in this PR for anyone debugging missing spans.

findings.title: No test covers the new eviction-on-insert behaviour
findings.body: The PR's headline change is trimming segments to 1000 spans during insert (`zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua) and the switch from sets to sorted sets scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, yet the only test changes are mechanical additions of `end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0` to existing fixtures. There is no test that pushes more than the limit of spans into one segment and asserts that the oldest-ending spans are the ones dropped, nor any test that the score is preserved correctly across the `zunionstore` merges. The previously-tested-by-implication span-count guard in `_load_segment_data` was removed with no replacement coverage, so a regression in the eviction logic (wrong aggregate, wrong pop count, off-by-one on the threshold) would go unnoticed.
